title: Gratitude

lines: LOOK HOW MUCH WORK WENT IN.
cards: Two guests leave the same dinner party. In the car, the first one says: did you see how much work went into that? The bread was homemade.
She set a place card with my name. She stayed up cooking for us. The second one says: honestly, it was just pasta.
I had one glass of wine. They'd have made dinner anyway. Same table, same food, same host.
The Talmud tells a version of this story, and the difference has a name.

teach.h: RECOGNIZE, LIKE A FACE IN A CROWD.
teach.b: Hakarat hatov. Recognizing the good. Four turns.
First, the phrase. It doesn't say feeling thankful. It says recognizing, the way you recognize a face in a crowd.
The good is already there; the work is to see it, and to see who did it.
Second, the two guests. In tractate Berakhot, the sage Ben Zoma describes them. The good guest says, in effect: how much trouble my host went to, and all of it for me.
The bad guest says: what trouble did he go to? I ate one piece of bread, one cup of wine, and whatever he did, he did for his own household. The meal didn't change.
The seeing did. Third, a word some teachers say means two things. Hodaah, giving thanks, can also mean admitting.
The short prayer some Jews say on waking begins modeh ani: I thank, or I acknowledge. Gratitude becomes a kind of confession: I didn't do this alone.
Fourth, people, not only God. Jewish prayer thanks God often.
Mussar adds that hakarat hatov points at people too: the parent who drove you, the teacher who stayed late, the stranger who held the door.
This is the other side of Salanter's water story: noticing the buckets someone carried for you. The second guest isn't a villain. He's tired, a little proud, and not looking.
Mussar asks for the first guest's eyes, one dinner at a time.

how: In Mussar practice, Jews work on hakarat hatov by noticing and naming specific kindnesses from other people, and the short morning prayer modeh ani begins the day with thanks.

s: hakarat hatov means feeling thankful inside
it means recognizing: seeing the good someone did, and who did it.
the Talmud tells of two guests at the same meal
Ben Zoma's good guest sees the host's trouble; the bad guest sees one piece of bread.
in this teaching, gratitude is only directed at God
Mussar points hakarat hatov at people too: parents, teachers, strangers.

games.q: you're leaving a friend's dinner. it was simple food, and you only had one plate. what do you say in the car?
o: it was just pasta; they'd have cooked anyway.
look how much trouble they went to, and all of it for us.
games.why: Ben Zoma's good guest says how much trouble the host went to for me. the bad guest, at the same meal, sees only one piece of bread.

practice: Look back over the last day or two, like the good guest in the car, and find one thing someone did for you that you barely noticed; name it, and name who did it.
Then a second, maybe a coffee made or a check-in text, and a third from long ago, someone who taught you to read, or drive, or cook, and for each one, picture the trouble it took them.
If you pray, give thanks for them in your own words; if not, hold each face for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Hakarat hatov. Recognizing the good: seeing what someone did for you, and the trouble it took, like Ben Zoma's good guest. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: recognize the good. Not just the gift, but the trouble it took. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 58a (Ben Zoma's good and bad guest)
